titulo: Exploring Bacterial Cellulose and a Biosurfactant as Eco-Friendly Strategies for Addressing Pharmaceutical Contaminants
titulo_curto: Bacterial cellulose to remove drugs and hormones from water

em_1_minuto.titulo: Drugs that end up in rivers
em_1_minuto.texto: Traces of medicines and hormones, such as those in birth control pills, reach the water and can cause harm even in very small amounts.
They tested membranes of cellulose made by bacteria, plain, freeze-dried or with a biosurfactant, to capture paracetamol and the hormone ethinylestradiol from water.
The cellulose captured up to 88% of the hormone and up to 31.8% of the paracetamol. The biosurfactant helped with paracetamol but hindered the hormone.
Bacterial cellulose is natural and biodegradable and can help remove hormones from contaminated water. The biosurfactant still needs fine-tuning.

secoes.lede: Painkillers, antibiotics, anti-inflammatories and hormones reach rivers through sewage and still lack well-defined safety limits.

blocos.html:
Industry and everyday city life release substances into water in tiny amounts, the micropollutants. Among them are drugs and natural and synthetic hormones, such as estrone, estradiol, estriol and ethinylestradiol. There is evidence of toxicity to aquatic life, hormonal disruption and even encouragement of antibiotic resistance.

There is still no consensus on which amounts are safe for the environment and human health.

itens.texto: Hormone found in birth control pills. Even at extremely low concentrations, it can disrupt animals' hormonal systems.
A widely used painkiller and fever reducer. In excess, it can damage the liver and kidneys; its long-term effects are hard to track.

blocos.html: One way to remove these substances is sorption: a porous material “pulls” the contaminant out of the water, either into itself (absorption) or onto its surface (adsorption). The study tested bacterial cellulose as this material and, for the first time, combined it with a biosurfactant, a kind of “natural soap” produced by the bacterium Bacillus subtilis.

secoes.lede: Three versions of the cellulose were immersed in contaminated water and monitored over time.

itens.texto: Whole bacterial cellulose membrane, with the surface water removed.
Membrane left for 24 hours in a biosurfactant solution to absorb it.
Cellulose frozen at −80 °C, freeze-dried for 48 hours and ground.
The bacterium Gluconacetobacter xylinus grew for 7 days at 30 °C in 24-well plates. The membranes were cleaned with caustic soda, washed and sterilized.
Bacillus subtilis grew for 96 hours at 35 °C. The biosurfactant was separated by centrifugation, acidification and solvent extraction, then freeze-dried.
An infrared (FTIR) analysis showed it had the same “chemical signatures” as standard surfactin and that it remained in the cellulose even after washing.
Samples of 0.5 g of cellulose were placed in 60 mL of water with paracetamol (2 g/L) or with the EE2 hormone (2 mg/L).

itens.titulo: Measure what was left in the water
itens.texto: Samples were taken from 10 minutes to 24 hours. Paracetamol was measured by spectrophotometry (430 nm) and the hormone by chromatography (HPLC).

secoes.titulo: How much of each contaminant the cellulose captured
secoes.lede: Choose the contaminant and compare the three versions of the cellulose.

parametros.leitura: The cellulose was very effective against the hormone, especially the freeze-dried version. With the biosurfactant, capture fell by almost half.
Paracetamol was harder to capture: most of it stayed in the water. Here the biosurfactant helped, and the freeze-dried cellulose had the best result.

blocos.nota: Highest percentage captured in each case (adsorption peak), according to the text of the paper.

blocos.alt: Three line graphs showing paracetamol concentration in the water falling and then rising over time

blocos.html: Time makes a difference. The cellulose captures the contaminant quickly, but then becomes “full” (saturated) and some of it goes back into the water. In the freeze-dried cellulose, for example, this release began after about 100 minutes. For the hormone, the best moment was at 20 minutes.

secoes.titulo: Why the biosurfactant helped one and hindered the other
secoes.lede: Surfactants change how molecules attach to surfaces, and the effect is not always predictable.

blocos.html:
Biosurfactants form small spheres (micelles) that can “wrap” the contaminant and shield it, changing its mobility. Earlier studies had already shown they can speed up or slow down pollutant cleanup, with no way to predict the result before testing. This helps explain the fast release seen in the cellulose with biosurfactant.

The attraction between the cellulose and the hormone probably involves hydrogen bonds and electrical forces, as already described for modified celluloses. By comparison, rice husk needed 120 minutes to best capture 17β-estradiol, while bacterial cellulose reached its best point with EE2 in 20 minutes.

secoes.titulo: What the study allows us to say
secoes.lede: A promising natural material against hormones in water.

blocos.html: The biosurfactant was successfully produced and incorporated into the cellulose. Freeze-dried cellulose was the most efficient at capturing the EE2 hormone, and the biosurfactant improved paracetamol capture but reduced hormone capture. Bacterial cellulose, especially freeze-dried, is a candidate eco-friendly biosorbent for removing certain drugs from polluted water.

itens: Adjust the biosurfactant concentration to improve capture without losing the cellulose's natural effectiveness.
Study the ideal contact time, since the contaminant can return to the water after saturation.

glossario.def: Substances present in water in tiny amounts, such as traces of drugs and hormones.
A substance that interferes with how hormones work in people and animals.
Synthetic hormone, similar to estrogen, used in birth control pills.
When a material removes a substance from a liquid, by absorption or adsorption.
When a substance sticks to the surface of a material.
The opposite of adsorption: the substance comes off the material and returns to the liquid.
A substance that acts like soap, produced by microbes. It is biodegradable.
Classic biosurfactant produced by Bacillus subtilis, used as a standard for comparison.
Drying at low temperature under vacuum, which removes water without damaging the material.
Infrared light analysis that identifies the chemical groups in a substance.
High-performance liquid chromatography: separates and measures substances in very small amounts.
Technique that measures how much of a substance is in a sample by the light it absorbs.
